title: Ext one of a direct sum is the product of Ext one
statement: Let $A$ be a commutative ring, let $N$ be an $A$-module, and let $(C_j)_{j\in J}$ be a family of $A$-modules. Put $P=\bigoplus_{j\in J}C_j$ [def-weil-pbc-direct-sum-modules], with canonical inclusions $\iota_j:C_j\to P$. For an $A$-module $Q$, define $\operatorname{Ext}^{1,\mathrm{ext}}_A(Q,N)$ to be the set of equivalence classes of short exact sequences $0\to N\xrightarrow{u}E\xrightarrow{v}Q\to0$ [def-weil-pbc-exact-sequence], where two sequences are equivalent when there is an $A$-module isomorphism $h:E\xrightarrow{\sim}E'$ with $h\circ u=u'$ and $v'\circ h=v$. For each $j$, pullback along $\iota_j$ sends the class of $(u,v)$ to the class of $0\to N\to E\mathbin{\times_P}C_j\to C_j\to0$, where $E\mathbin{\times_P}C_j=\{(e,c)\mid v(e)=\iota_j(c)\}$. The resulting map $\Phi_A: \operatorname{Ext}^{1,\mathrm{ext}}_A(P,N)\to\prod_{j\in J}\operatorname{Ext}^{1,\mathrm{ext}}_A(C_j,N)$, $[E]\mapsto([E\mathbin{\times_P}C_j])_{j\in J}$, is a bijection.

source.place: proof of Lemma Tag 05EG (lemma-neighbourhood-extensions), lines 24504-24516: compatibility of Ext with direct sums

proof.text: For an extension $0\to N\xrightarrow{u}E\xrightarrow{v}P\to0$ and an inclusion $\iota_j:C_j\to P$, the pullback is $E\times_P C_j=\{(e,c)\mid v(e)=\iota_j(c)\}$ with its evident maps from $N$ and to $C_j$. An equivalence of extensions induces an equivalence of these pullbacks, so $\Phi_A$ is well-defined.

To prove surjectivity, choose representatives $0\to N\xrightarrow{u_j}E_j\xrightarrow{v_j}C_j\to0$ of a tuple of classes. The direct-sum map $p:\bigoplus_jE_j\to P$ is surjective, and its kernel is exactly $\bigoplus_j u_j(N)$: an element has finite support, and each component lies in $\ker(v_j)=\operatorname{im}(u_j)$ precisely when it lies in the kernel. Let $\Sigma:\bigoplus_jN\to N$ be the finite-sum map. In Lean, the range and kernel formulas for DFinsupp.mapRange.linearMap prove exactness of the componentwise direct-sum maps; DirectSum.lmap_injective and DirectSum.lmap_surjective give the endpoint properties.

Form $E=(N\oplus\bigoplus_jE_j)/R$, where $R$ is the image of $\bigoplus_jN\to N\oplus\bigoplus_jE_j$, $n\mapsto(\Sigma(n),-\bigoplus_j u_j(n_j))$. The maps $N\to E$, $a\mapsto[(a,0)]$, and $E\to P$, $[(a,e)]\mapsto p(e)$ are well-defined. The first is injective, the second is surjective, and if $p(e)=0$ then $e=\bigoplus_j u_j(n_j)$, so $[(0,e)]=[(\Sigma(n),0)]$; hence their image and kernel agree. Thus $0\to N\to E\to P\to0$ is short exact by the cited definition. The quotient universal property also yields a linear map to any module G from compatible maps N → G and E_j → G agreeing on each copy of N. Maps from this quotient to P are determined by their restrictions to N and the E_j.

The compatible maps t_j:E_j→E from the quotient construction induce maps E_j→E×_P C_j by e↦(t_j(e),v_j(e)). Each pullback sequence is short exact: its projection is surjective by lifting along E→P, its kernel is the copy of N by exactness of E, and the map from N is injective. The induced map fixes N and C_j. An elementary short-five-lemma argument proves that it is bijective: an element of its kernel lies in N and is zero by endpoint injectivity; to lift an element, first lift its C_j-coordinate and then correct the difference by an element of N. Its inverse is the required pullback equivalence. Finally shrink E to universe max(w,x,y): a set-theoretic section of E→P gives a surjection N×P→E, so E is small in the universe of its endpoints. Transport the module structure and all maps along Shrink.linearEquiv. No arbitrary unproved existence witness is used.

For injectivity, form the pullback extensions E_j=F×_P C_j of the first extension F. Apply the same explicit quotient construction to these short exact sequences to obtain 0→N→G→P→0 with maps t_j:E_j→G and the quotient universal property. The canonical projections E_j→F and their composites E_j→F' with the given endpoint-fixed pullback equivalences agree on N.

Apply the quotient universal property with target F×F' to obtain a linear map G→F×F'; its components f:G→F and f':G→F' fix N. Their composites to P agree with G→P because maps from G to P are determined by N and the E_j, and the given pullback equivalences fix the C_j coordinates. The elementary short-five-lemma argument from the surjectivity part proves that f and f' are bijective. Thus f'∘f⁻¹:F→F' is a linear isomorphism fixing N and commuting with the maps to P. This proves injectivity without a separate choice of inverse pullback equivalences.
A well-defined map that is both surjective and injective is a bijection, so $\Phi_A$ has the asserted bijectivity.
